                          KEVIN KENNEDY AND JOHN BURROW’S
                                     RESPONSE TO REMAND



      REQUEST FOR INDEPENDENT INVESTIGATION AND FORENSIC AUDIT

         In accordance with Commission Advising memorandums (59475-6558) filed on
September 9, 2026, Kevin Kennedy ("Mr. Kennedy”) and John Burrow (“Mr. Burrow”), both pro
se intervenors, respectfully file this response to Chairman Gleeson’s memorandum dated
September 9, 2026 regarding remand of State Office of Administrative Hearings (“SOAH”)
Administrative Law Judges’ (“ALJs’ ”) Proposal For Decision (“PFD”) for Dockets 59182 and
59475.
         Mr. Kennedy and Mr. Burrow ask the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission)
to act upon this request or the ALJs to recommend action through immediate commencement of
an independent investigation of the validity of ERCOT modeling used in the Permian Basin
Reliability Plan (“PBRP”).
         To the best of our knowledge, the information referenced in this request has been
previously introduced into the record.




Kennedy-Burrow 59475 – Response to remand – audit request                               Page 1 of 24
     REQUEST FOR COMMISSION TO ORDER AN INDEPENDENT TECHNICAL
   INVESTIGATION AND FORENSIC AUDIT OF ERCOT’S 2024 PERMIAN BASIN
                    RELIABILITY PLAN MODELING



Dear Chairman Gleeson and Commissioners:

        Texas is preparing to spend roughly $11-billion to construct over 1,200 miles of 765-kV
transmission lines based on ERCOT’s Permian Basin 2024 computer model, a computer model
whose data input now raises serious questions regarding federal compliance.

        During 2024, ERCOT planners appear to have created two very different models of the
future Texas electric grid, for two different purposes, at the same time. One computer model, the
2024 Permian Reliability Plan, had questionable and possibly inaccurate assumptions. That
model was used to justify the three enormous 765-kV import paths, each stretching 400 miles
across Texas. Simultaneously, ERCOT had a second 2024 computer model that used
dramatically different growth assumptions about where future statewide electric demand and
generation would be located.

        ----- Did the 2024 Permian model discover the need for the 765 lines --- or --- did the
desire for the 765 lines create the demand and generation assumptions ERCOT put into the
Permian model? -----

        We are not accusing ERCOT of “cooking the books”. We are saying the differences in
the models are too significant to ignore and they must be investigated. Your decisions give utility
companies eminent domain authority over thousands of Texas landowners, affect tens of
thousands of acres, and place billions of dollars in costs on the backs of Texas ratepayers.

        Texas law recognizes that utilities operate as monopolies in the areas they serve and that
regulation is necessary to protect the public interest. When credible evidence raises serious
questions about the models being used to justify roughly $11 billion in transmission projects, a
request for independent verification is not an attack on you, ERCOT, or the utilities, it is
necessary regulatory oversight. This is exactly why the Public Utility Commission exists.

        Lt. Governor Patrick just raised a red flag on ERCOT executive compensation. Texans
demand the same accountability on something that is 2,000 times larger.

        We need you, or Governor Abbott, or Lt. Governor Patrick, or someone to see this red
flag we now raise and to take action to ensure the public interest is protected.

Kennedy-Burrow 59475 – Response to remand – audit request                                 Page 2 of 24
         Order a forensic audit, open the model, follow the data, verify NERC compliance, and
determine whether these lines are truly necessary.

        Shrugging your shoulders and saying “c'est la vie” is not an option.

        The following Request for Independent Investigation and Forensic Audit is a roadmap for
ERCOT accountability and transparency. We ask that you use it as the basis for the scope of your
investigation.

        If the Permian model is sound, an investigation will prove it. If it isn't, decision makers
and Texans deserve to know before billions are spent and irreparable harm is done to
generational family lands dating as far back as the 1800’s.

Very truly yours,
Kevin Kennedy           John M. Burrow
Bertram, TX             Salado, TX




                                I.      PURPOSE OF THIS REQUEST

        This memorandum respectfully requests that the Public Utility Commission of Texas
(“Commission”) direct an independent technical and forensic investigation and audit of the
topology modeling used by the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc. (“ERCOT”) in
developing the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (“PBRP”).

        Through the application processes for the five PBRP 765-kV transmission projects’
certificates of convenience and necessity (CCNs), but especially PUC Docket 59475 – Bell
County East to Big Hill, substantial credible evidence of a compelling nature has been brought to
light that raises legitimate concerns about the overall validity of the grid system topology model
that ERCOT used as the foundation of the PBRP and its 765-kV import paths recommendations.

        Figures 1 and 2 on the following page provide the immediately apparent need for an
independent audit. By what reasoning did ERCOT develop two totally different models,
simultaneously, side-by-side, one for their 2024 PBRP and another their 2024-RTP?




Kennedy-Burrow 59475 – Response to remand – audit request                                  Page 3 of 24
 Kennedy-Burrow 59475 – Response to remand – audit request   Page 4 of 24
         The central issues are:

              Did ERCOT use an appropriate temporally and spatially consistent system-wide
                model with sufficiently comprehensive transmission topology to properly
                determine the need and configuration of the three 765-kV Permian Basin import
                paths, ---or--- could ERCOT’s PBRP model selective assumptions and topology
                have materially affected the modeled power-flow distribution, transfer capability,
                contingency performance, and resulting transmission-need determinations?

              Did ERCOT’s PBRP model comply with required state and federal standards,
                including North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) Reliability
                Standard TPL-001-5.1?

        The requested independent investigation should determine whether the PBRP’s
underlying power-flow models used proper, contemporaneous, system-wide load and generation
data; whether the models were internally consistent with the modeling-data requirements
applicable to ERCOT and its Transmission Planners; whether the models complied with the
federal requirements of NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1 applicable during 2024,
particularly Requirements R1, R2, and R3; and, ultimately, whether the reliability violations and
import transmission needs identified by the PBRP remain valid when evaluated using an
appropriately reconciled and contemporaneous system-wide model.

        This request most certainly does not allege and does not ask the Commission to presume
that ERCOT “cooked the books” or that they violated a NERC Reliability Standard, rather, it
asks the Commission to obtain an independent determination of whether the modeling practices
used in the PBRP were consistent with the applicable reliability and modeling requirements and
whether the resulting transmission recommendations are sufficiently supported by technically
appropriate system-wide modeling.

        Ultimately, are the PBRP 765-kV Import Paths the result of a flawed model? Does the
Commission simply shrug its shoulders and move on or are the citizens of Texas worthy of the
time necessary for a second, independent opinion?




Kennedy-Burrow 59475 – Response to remand – audit request                               Page 5 of 24
                                          II.     BACKGROUND

        In December 2023, the Commission directed ERCOT to develop a reliability plan for the
Permian Basin pursuant to HB 5066 and PURA §39.167. The Commission’s procedural schedule
contemplated that applicable transmission service providers (TSPs) would provide the necessary
load demand data in January 2024 and that ERCOT would develop the reliability plan during the
ensuing months. ERCOT subsequently developed the PBRP and filed its study with the
Commission in July 2024.
        The PBRP modeled future needs for 2030 and 2038 and identified recommendations
based on that modeling, which ERCOT divided those proposed upgrades into two categories:

              Local transmission upgrades to interconnect and serve the projected load in the
                Permian Basin region assuming that power can be imported into the region.

              Import paths or new long-haul transmission lines to transfer bulk power to the
                Permian Basin from other regions of the state. ERCOT provided analysis and
                recommendation of three import options made up of three different voltage
                regimes: 345-kV, 500-kV, and 765-kV.

        The Commission approved the local project portion of the PBRP in October 2024 but
deferred a decision on the import paths. In April 2025, The Commission approved the 765-kV
import option, which consisted of three import paths totaling 1,255 miles. The proposed 765-kV
import paths all generally originated along the Interstate 35 corridor, as depicted in Figure 1.

        Concurrently with the development of the PBRP, ERCOT developed its 2024 Regional
Transmission Plan (2024-RTP) modeling. ERCOT describes the 2024-RTP as a “coordinated
planning process performed by ERCOT Grid Planning with extensive review and input by
Transmission Planners (TPs) and Transmission Owners (TOs) registered with North American
Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC), and other stakeholders. The 2024 RTP addresses
ERCOT System transmission needs for years 2026 through 2030. This report documents the
results of the assessment, in part, to comply with the requirements of NERC Reliability
Standards, ERCOT Protocols, and the ERCOT Planning Guide.”
        Both the PBRP and the 2024-RTP would seemingly have required full, system-wide 2030
models to properly balance necessary added generation supplies with forecasted 2030 load
demands, identify reliability violations, and to be able to make recommendations for


Kennedy-Burrow 59475 – Response to remand – audit request                                 Page 6 of 24
 improvements that would be based on sound engineering principles, would be able to withstand
scrutiny, and would comply with the federal requirements of NERC Reliability Standards.
        ERCOTs 2030 PBRP modeling inputs appear to vary greatly from the 2030 modeling
inputs ERCOT used for its 2024-RTP, even though the two models were built and analyzed
contemporaneously, drawing input from the same universe of known, available 2030 data.
        The concern addressed by this request is not the Legislative decision to mandate a
Permian Basin reliability plan. The concern is the integrity and consistency of the system-wide
modeling inputs used to identify the reliability deficiencies and the transmission project
recommendations contained in ERCOT’s Permian Basin Reliability Plan, notably the 765-
kV import path recommendations.


             III.   ERCOT’S TWO DIFFFERENT 2024 SYSTEM-WIDE MODELS

        The publicly available modeling information indicates that ERCOT was simultaneously
performing the 2024-RTP and the PBRP during substantially the same period in 2024, but two
studies appear to have used materially different distributions of load and generation despite both
being system-wide models.
        The issue identified for investigation is not simply that ERCOT maintained two models.
Multiple models can be entirely legitimate when they represent different study years, regions,
seasons, scenarios, sensitivities, or planning objectives. The concern is that the two models
appear to contain materially different temporal and spatial distributions of load and generation,
while both were used to evaluate reliability and bulk transmission needs utilizing a system-wide
model and data analysis.


        PBRP:
        The principal concern is that the PBRP appears to have incorporated newer and
        substantially increased 2024 TSP forecasted load information only in the Permian Basin
        region while significant portions of the load representation outside the Permian Basin
        appears to have remained based on earlier 2023 forecast information, associated with the
        2023-RTP.
        Thus, the PBRP seems to contain a mixture of:

              Newer, larger load forecasts in the Permian Basin;


Kennedy-Burrow 59475 – Response to remand – audit request                                Page 7 of 24
               Older, smaller load forecasts for other portions of the ERCOT system; and
              System-wide geographic distributions of added future generation located
                predominantly in eastern portions of the state (See Figure 1);

        PBRP skewed system-wide power-transfer conditions may have resulted from ERCOT’s
        apparent combination of asymmetric load-demand inputs.


        2024-RTP:
                The 2024-RTP model inputs seem to be markedly different from that of the
        PBRP. It appears the 2024-RTP included all available 2024 TSP forecasted load
        information, throughout the entire system. The exact difference between the 2024 TSP
        loads included in the PBRP and the 2024-RTP is difficult to ascertain through publicly
        available information but the difference in added future generation included in the two
        models may provide a reasonable estimate of the difference in TSP load demand; PBRP:
        17,000-MW and 2024-RTP: 59,000-MW. The generation difference was 42,000-MW,
        presumably 42,000-MW for 2038 but possibly 45,000-MW for 2030. Figure 2 depicts the
        system-wide distribution of the added future generation in the 2024-RTP, which paints a
        stark realization of the differences between the PBRP model and the 2024-RTP model
        when Figure 1 and Figure 2 are compared.

        The discrepancies must be reconciled:
                This creates a question that cannot be resolved simply by determining whether
        each individual load forecast was accurate in isolation. The relevant question is whether
        each system as modeled was internally consistent as a representation of a particular
        projected and reasonably anticipated system condition.
                In other words, how could both the PBRP’s 2030 modeling and the 2024-RTP’s
        2030 modeling be true reflections of what ERCOT expected as their 2030 system
        condition? If one was not a complete representation of expected 2030 conditions, how
        can its system-wide bulk transfer findings be considered accurate and reliable?




Kennedy-Burrow 59475 – Response to remand – audit request                                 Page 8 of 24
           IV.      WHY THE TEMPORAL AND SPATIAL DIFFERENCES REQUIRE
                                               INVESTIGATION

        The Permian Basin is not isolated. ----- Electric transmission reliability can be
determined by behaviors anywhere within the interconnected system. Changing conditions at a
particular location causes ripple effects throughout the system; the larger the change, the greater
the ripple.
        Changes in load and generation anywhere on the interconnected system can alter:

               real-power transfers;
               reactive-power flows;
               transmission-line loading;
               interface loading;
               bus voltages;
               generator dispatch;
               reactive-resource requirements; and
               the severity and location of contingency violations.

        Consequently, introducing materially newer load forecasts into one geographic area while
retaining older forecasts elsewhere can change the modeled system-wide power-flow condition.


        The same issue applies to generation. ----- If additional Permian Basin load was
accompanied by additional generation that was predominantly located outside the Permian Basin,
the geographic placement of that generation could materially affect the modeled transmission
transfers and therefore the transmission facilities identified as necessary.
        Accordingly, the investigation should determine whether the differences between the two
models (PBRP and 2024-RTP) represent:
              a. legitimate and documented sensitivity cases;
              b. different planning horizons or planning objectives;
              c. studied stress conditions;
              d. a mixture of forecast vintages and geographically differentiated inputs that was
                 used to make system-wide reliability and transmission-planning determinations
                 without an adequate technical basis for treating the resulting model as a
                 representative system-wide planning condition.

Kennedy-Burrow 59475 – Response to remand – audit request                                    Page 9 of 24
         To what extent were the calculated 765-kV import flows determined by actual (and
complete) anticipated forecast conditions, and to what extent were they determined by the spatial
and temporal structure of the PBRP model inputs? --This should be answered quantitatively. --


         V.     THE SCALE OF THE IMPORT PATHS CHANGES THE MODELING
                                                   QUESTION

The PBRP demonstrates the geographic scale of these facilities.

        For the 765-kV import path alternative:
               Import Path 1: approximately 442 miles.
               Import Path 2: approximately 443 miles.
               Import Path 3: approximately 370 miles.

        Collectively, the three 765-kV paths require approximately 1,255 miles of new bulk
transmission lines.
        Accordingly, if the PBRP sensitivity analysis was principally performed against the local
Permian projects, but the resulting conclusions were subsequently used to establish the need for
import paths, the Commission should determine whether the system-wide consequences of the
asymmetric model inputs were independently tested as appropriate for the import-path analysis.
        The investigation should specifically answer:
                Were the same temporal and spatial load and generation assumptions used to
        evaluate the need for the import paths as were used to evaluate the local Permian
        projects?
                If the answer is yes, the auditor should determine whether those assumptions
        were appropriate for a system-wide import-path analysis. Were the PBRP system-wide
        load and generation assumptions consistent with all known and available data?
                If the answer is no, the auditor should determine:
                      a. What model was used for the import-path analysis?
                      b. What system-wide load assumptions were used?
                      c. What system-wide generation assumptions were used?
                      d. What system transfer assumptions were used?
                      e. What forecast vintage was used for each geographic region?



Kennedy-Burrow 59475 – Response to remand – audit request                             Page 10 of 24
                     f. Whether the import-path analysis used the same PBRP base case as the
                        local-project analysis.
                    g. Whether the 2024 RTP model data was used or considered. If not, why
                        not?
                    h. Whether a sensitivity analysis was performed on the import paths.
                    i. Whether the import-path restudied under the 2024 RTP load and
                        generation assumptions or were the import paths simply inserted into the
                        2024-RTP base case with alternative analysis.
                    j. Whether the geographic distribution of generation may have materially
                        affected the identified import requirements.



                      VI.      REQUIRED NERC TPL-001-5.1 COMPLIANCE

        NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1 was effective during 2024 and was therefore a
required federal standard during the PBRP/2024-RTP modeling period.
        Requirement R1 provides that Transmission Planners and Planning Coordinators,
including ERCOT, must maintain system models for the studies necessary to complete the
Planning Assessment. Critically, those models must use data consistent with the data provided
pursuant to MOD-032 and must represent projected system conditions. R1.1 further identifies,
among other things, real and reactive load forecasts and resources required for load as
information that the models must represent.
        Requirement R2 requires an annual Planning Assessment and specifies the use of current
or qualified past studies. The standard also requires sensitivity cases to demonstrate the impact of
changes to basic assumptions and requires the relevant assumptions and results to be
documented.
        Requirement R3 is particularly relevant to this inquiry. It requires the steady-state
Planning Assessment studies to be based on computer simulation models using the data provided
in Requirement R1. The studies must then evaluate specified planning events and extreme events
against the applicable performance requirements.
        It does not appear ERCOT’s PBRP used consistent model input or that ERCOT
conducted the required steady-state analysis of import paths in the PBRP. ----- Accordingly, the
requested audit should not merely ask whether the PBRP model produced mathematically correct


Kennedy-Burrow 59475 – Response to remand – audit request                                 Page 11 of 24
 power-flow solutions. It should determine whether the inputs to the model were appropriate
and compliant with the federal data and modeling requirements of NERC that govern
planning studies.


        NERC MOD-032-1 (Input data quality and consistency)
                MOD-032-1 is the NERC standard specifically addressing data for power-system
        modeling and analysis. Its stated purpose is to establish consistent modeling-data
        requirements and reporting procedures for development of planning-horizon cases
        necessary to analyze the reliability of the interconnected transmission system.
                MOD-032-1 R1 requires the Planning Coordinator and Transmission Planners to
        jointly establish modeling-data requirements and reporting procedures addressing steady-
        state, dynamics, and short-circuit modeling data, including case types or scenarios and
        the schedule for submission of data.
                R2 requires applicable entities, including entities such as Load Serving Entities,
        Transmission Owners, Transmission Service Providers, and other specified registered
        entities, to provide the required modeling data according to those procedures.
                R3 provides a mechanism for the Planning Coordinator or Transmission Planner
        to raise technical concerns regarding submitted data and requires the affected entity either
        to provide updated data or provide a technically supported explanation for maintaining
        the existing data.
                The technical rationale underlying MOD-032-1 specifically recognizes that
        modeling data must be correct, periodically checked, and updated, and identifies
        load data as information that can change as improved forecasts become available.


ERCOT’s PBRP model data does appear to be consistent with ERCOT’s 2024-RTP model data.
----- For this and other reasons, the audit should examine not only the final PBRP model, but the
data-collection, data-selection, data-update, data-freeze, and model-construction processes that
produced it.

        NERC MOD-033-1 (Steady-state and dynamic analyses)
                NERC MOD-033-1 is the NERC standard addressing steady-state and dynamic
        system model validation. Its purpose is to establish requirements for validating planning




Kennedy-Burrow 59475 – Response to remand – audit request                                 Page 12 of 24
         models so that the models reasonably represent actual system behavior and can be relied
        upon for planning and reliability analysis.
                MOD-033-1 requires the Planning Coordinator to establish and implement a
        documented model-validation process addressing both steady-state and dynamic system
        behavior. The validation process includes comparing modeled system performance
        against actual system behavior and identifying material discrepancies between the model
        and the actual system.
                The standard requires validation of the planning model using appropriate real-
        world system data, including comparison of modeled steady-state results with actual
        system conditions. Where differences between the model and actual system behavior are
        identified, the validation process is intended to determine whether the differences are
        acceptable or require investigation and correction.
                The technical rationale underlying MOD-033 recognizes that planning models
        must be validated against actual system behavior because inaccurate or incomplete
        models can produce misleading reliability assessments, including inaccurate
        identification of system limitations, violations, and transmission needs.


        ERCOT’s PBRP seems to indicate that no steady-state analysis was performed on the
import paths. ----- For this and other reasons, the audit should examine not merely whether
ERCOT had a model-validation process, but whether the specific model used for the PBRP was
validated, what actual system data was used for that validation, what discrepancies were
identified, and whether material discrepancies involving load, generation, topology, or power
flows were resolved before ERCOT relied upon the PBRP results to identify reliability violations
and recommend major transmission facilities.
        Limited dynamic analysis is not a substitute for required steady-state analysis
                The PBRP materials identify a limited dynamic stability analysis associated with
        the 765-kV import path alternatives.
                The auditor should therefore separately identify:
                    a. Need analysis
                                 What established the need for the 765-kV import paths?
                    b. Steady-state analysis
                                 What established their thermal and voltage performance?



Kennedy-Burrow 59475 – Response to remand – audit request                                 Page 13 of 24
                     c. Dynamic analysis
                                What established their dynamic stability?
                These are different engineering questions. The auditor should obtain the actual
        study files supporting each conclusion.


                  VII. IMPORT PATH QUESTIONS UNDER TPL-001-5.1 R2

        The auditor should specifically determine whether the PBRP treated the import paths as
merely the consequence of a local Permian sensitivity or as an independently demonstrated
system-wide transmission requirement.
        This distinction matters because R2.1.3 specifically recognizes expected transfers as a
sensitivity variable.
        The Commission should therefore require the auditor to reconstruct at least three
analytical conditions:
                Case 1 — PBRP Base Case
                         Reproduce the actual PBRP model and results.
                Case 2 — PBRP Reconciled Case
                         Retain the PBRP’s intended Permian load forecast but replace inconsistent
                         load and generation inputs elsewhere with the contemporaneous system-
                         wide assumptions appropriate to the same planning horizon.
                Case 3 — 2024 RTP Case
                         Use the contemporaneous 2024 RTP system-wide load and generation
                         assumptions, while evaluating the Permian reliability condition and the
                         proposed import paths.


        The auditor should then compare:
              thermal violations;
              voltage violations;
              transfer capability;
              limiting elements;
              contingency severity;
              required import capacity;


Kennedy-Burrow 59475 – Response to remand – audit request                               Page 14 of 24
               required number of import paths;
              proposed voltage level; and
              proposed transmission facilities.
        This would provide an empirical answer to whether the import paths are robust to
reconciliation of the underlying system-wide assumptions.


        Possible “Local Sensitivity” Defense Should Be Tested, Not Assumed
                ERCOT could reasonably contend that the PBRP was a special-purpose study
        focused on exceptional load growth in the Permian Basin region. That explanation should
        be tested rather than accepted.
                The auditor should ask:
                         If the PBRP was intended to function as a geographically constrained
                reliability study, where does ERCOT identify that limitation in the study
                methodology, and how did ERCOT transition from that localized sensitivity to
                system-wide conclusions regarding hundreds of miles of import path
                transmission?


                Conversely:
                         If ERCOT intended the PBRP model to represent the system-wide
                planning condition for purposes of evaluating cross-state import paths, why were
                temporally and spatially different load and generation assumptions used rather
                than those contained in the contemporaneous 2024-RTP?
                Either answer provides a testable audit question.


           VIII. INDIVIDUAL IMPORT PATH TESTING UNDER TPL-001-5.1 R2

        The three approved paths should each receive an independent analysis.
        Import Path 1:
                The auditor should identify:
                        modeled source;
                        modeled sink;
                        load served;
                        generation assumptions;

Kennedy-Burrow 59475 – Response to remand – audit request                              Page 15 of 24
                          steady-state violations;
                         dynamic contingencies;
                         transfer capability;
                         limiting elements;
                         model version;
                         forecast vintage; and
                         whether the path remains necessary under the reconciled model.
        Import Path 2:
                  The same analysis should be performed independently.
        Import Path 3:
                  The same analysis should be performed independently.


        The auditor should then determine whether all three paths are independently required or
whether their need depends upon the combined assumptions of the PBRP model.


         IX.      STEADY-STATE ANALYSIS OF THE IMPORT PATHS SHOULD BE
                                                     PRODUCED

        The Commission should obtain the actual steady-state study files supporting the 765-kV
import-path recommendations.
        The audit should identify:
                every base case;
                every contingency;
                every monitored element;
                every violation;
                every limiting element;
                every path transfer limit;
                every voltage violation;
                every thermal violation;
                every remedial transmission project;
                every generation redispatch assumption; and
                every assumption regarding the three import paths.


Kennedy-Burrow 59475 – Response to remand – audit request                             Page 16 of 24
         The audit should determine whether the 765-kV import paths themselves were subjected
to the same comprehensive steady-state contingency analysis as the local Permian projects and
the later used in the 2024 RTP, as required by federal standards including NERC TPL-001-5.1.


                   X.     NERC MODELING AND PLANNING COMPLIANCE

        The auditor should determine whether the PBRP modeling and planning process
complied with the applicable NERC requirements in effect during 2024, including:
              TPL-001-5.1;
              MOD-032; and
              MOD-033.


        The investigation should not assume a violation. Instead, it should determine:
            a. what data was required;
            b. what data was submitted;
            c. what data ERCOT used;
            d. what validation occurred;
            e. whether discrepancies existed;
            f. whether the PBRP model was validated;
            g. whether the model was consistent with other contemporaneous planning models;
            h. whether the differences were material; and
            i. whether any resulting issue warrants referral to NERC’s compliance process.



             XI.    THE AUDIT SHOULD DETERMINE WHETHER THE 765-KV
               RECOMMENDATION WAS PREMATURELY EMBEDDED IN LATER
                                                   MODELING

        This is particularly important because ERCOT’s subsequent 2024-RTP 765-kV analysis
states that its start case incorporated the three PBRP 765-kV import paths while a September 20,
2024 letter from ERCOT Vice President, Ms. Katie Hobbs to the Commission stated: “Upon
further internal evaluation, however, ERCOT now believes that identifying the specific




Kennedy-Burrow 59475 – Response to remand – audit request                                Page 17 of 24
 transmission facility elements that could be utilized for either 345-kV or 765-kV import options
would require further engineering study by ERCOT's planning department”.
        ERCOT stated the PBRP’s 765-kV import options needed further study, was that done or
did the 2024-RTP treat the PBRP 765-kV lines as a given?
        The auditor should therefore determine:
            a. Were the PBRP 765-kV paths treated as assumed facilities in the later 2024-RTP?
            b. Were they removed and tested as alternatives, individually or grouped?
            c. Were the later reliability findings dependent upon those facilities already being in
                service?
            d. Did the later 2024-RTP independently establish the need for the import paths?
            e. Did the later study effectively inherit the PBRP’s assumptions and treat the PBRP
                import paths as if they were existing facilities?


        This is an important potential “self-fulfilling” question.
              If PBRP establishes need for 765-kV paths,
              and then the 2024-RTP assumes the PBRP paths exist as its starting topology,
              the auditor should determine whether the 2024-RTP independently validated the

        The Permian Basin is not isolated. ----- Electric transmission reliability can be
determined by behaviors anywhere within the interconnected system. Changing conditions at a
particular location causes ripple effects throughout the system; the larger the change, the greater
the ripple.
        Changes in load and generation anywhere on the interconnected system can alter:

              • real-power transfers;
              • reactive-power flows;
              • transmission-line loading;
              • interface loading;
              • bus voltages;
              • generator dispatch;
              • reactive-resource requirements; and
              • the severity and location of contingency violations.

        Consequently, introducing materially newer load forecasts into one geographic area while
retaining older forecasts elsewhere can change the modeled system-wide power-flow condition.


        The same issue applies to generation. ----- If additional Permian Basin load was
accompanied by additional generation that was predominantly located outside the Permian Basin,
the geographic placement of that generation could materially affect the modeled transmission
transfers and therefore the transmission facilities identified as necessary.
